section_1.title: Prerequisite Refresh: The Static Slope
section_1.content: Recall the slope formula (rise over run). Visualize a static staircase. The derivative starts here: what happens when the 'stairs' become a smooth, curving ramp?
section_1.example: A static mountain profile shown on a coordinate plane, with a straight ruler measuring the steepness at a single, fixed point.

section_2.title: The Dynamic Transition: Zooming In
section_2.content: Introduce the 'Microscopic View.' Explain that a derivative is not just a slope, but a transformation that zooms into a curve until it looks like a straight line. The derivative is the 'local linear version' of any complex function.
section_2.example: An animation of a zooming lens focusing on a single point of a complex roller-coaster track, showing the curve flattening into a tangent line.

section_3.title: The 'Operator' View: Derivatives as Transformation
section_3.content: Shift the perspective: The derivative is an operator (d/dx) that transforms a function into a new function representing 'sensitivity.' If the input moves slightly, how much does the output shift?
section_3.example: A 'Robot Chef' (the operator) takes a raw ingredient (the function, like position) and transforms it into a seasoning (the derivative, velocity) that describes how fast the taste changes.

section_4.title: Application: The Cheetah’s Acceleration
section_4.content: Apply the transformational view to motion. If position is the function, the derivative transforms it into velocity. If velocity is the function, the derivative transforms it into acceleration.
section_4.example: A cheetah chasing a gazelle: The graph of position (distance) transforms into the graph of velocity (speed), visually showing the derivative's role in describing the cheetah's change in intensity.

section_5.title: Summary: The Derivative as a Lens
section_5.content: Conclude that the derivative is not just a number, but a transformation tool that maps 'State' to 'Change.' This is the foundation for modeling all dynamic systems in nature.
section_5.example: A final visual summary showing three layers: The Function (the object), the Derivative (the 'change-meter'), and the Result (predicted future state).
